item.title: Hot spatula burns, chilli powder in eyes: Chargesheet reveals abuse of domestic worker at former Biman MD’s home
item.description:
“They used to lock me in the bathroom”, “they burnt my neck with a hot spatula”, “they broke my teeth with a pestle”, and “they used to sprinkle chilli powder into my eyes” — these are the allegations of abuse made by an 11-year-old girl who worked as a domestic worker at the home of Safiqur Rahman, former managing director of Biman Bangladesh Airlines.

The girl also said that whenever her father visited her, the family made her wear oversized clothes to conceal the marks of abuse on her body.

The police have included the girl’s account in a charge sheet submitted to the court. On 31 August, Rubel Mia, the investigating officer and a sub-inspector (SI) of Uttara West police station, filed the charge sheet with a Dhaka court. It names Shafiqul Rahman, his wife, Bithi Akter, and two domestic workers at the house, Rupali Khatun and Sufia Begum, as accused.

The court has accepted the charge sheet and sent the case to Judge Sohel Rana of the 7th Women and Children Repression Prevention Tribunal in Dhaka for trial.

Rubel Mia, the investigating officer and an SI (Sub-Inspector) at Uttara West police station, told Prothom Alo, “I found the allegations to be substantiated during the investigation and included the findings in the charge sheet. Two of the accused admitted to the abuse in their statements.”

The alleged abuse came to light on 31 January, when the girl’s father took her from the home of Safiqur Rahman, the former managing director (MD) of Biman Bangladesh Airlines, and admitted her to hospital. The following day, 1 February, her father filed a case alleging that the accused had tortured his daughter.

The case names Shafiqul Rahman, his wife, Bithi Akter, and the two other domestic workers at the house, Rupali Khatun and Sufia Begum.

According to the case statement and accounts from the girl’s relatives, Jahangir, a security guard at Safiqur Rahman’s home in Sector 9 of Uttara, Dhaka, arranged for the 11-year-old girl to work there and look after the younger children.

Her father, who worked at a hotel, sent her to the house in June last year after receiving assurances that the family would cover the costs of her marriage and other expenses.

The case statement further says that the father last visited his daughter at the house on 2 November last year. After that, the family did not allow her to meet her relatives. On 31 January this year, Safiqur Rahman’s wife telephoned the father, informed him that the girl was ill and asked him to take her home.

When he arrived to collect his daughter, he noticed marks of abuse on her body. According to the case statement, he then admitted her to Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Medical College Hospital in Gazipur.

Police arrested all four accused that night following the father’s complaint. Safiqur Rahman, the former Biman MD, and domestic worker Rupali Khatun were subsequently released on bail. Bithi Akter, Safiqur Rahman’s wife, and the other domestic worker, Sufia Begum, remain in custody.

On 8 February, the girl gave a statement before the court of Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Nazmin Akter. The charge sheet includes her account of the alleged abuse.

In her statement, the girl said she had worked at Safiqur Rahman’s home for eight months. Her duties included looking after the “MD sir’s” child and picking up anything the child dropped on the floor. However, she alleged that Bithi Akter, the female head of the household, had beaten and tortured her from the time she arrived.

According to the girl’s statement, as cited in the charge sheet, Bithi Akter burnt various parts of her body with a hot spatula. When the girl screamed, she beat her with bamboo sticks and struck her thighs, both arms and back. She also sprinkled chilli powder into the girl’s eyes.

The girl further stated that, at one point, the accused broke her teeth using a pestle. She also alleged that the two other domestic workers at the house abused her.

Citing the girl’s account, the IO stated in the charge sheet that the family locked her in the bathroom. In an attempt to survive, she even drank water from the toilet and ate toothpaste.

What the charge sheet says about Safiqur’s role

The charge sheet also brings allegations against Safiqur Rahman, the former managing director of Biman Bangladesh Airlines. It states that his wife tortured the child for days on end, while he pretended not to notice despite witnessing the abuse. The IO noted that Safiqur could not evade responsibility for his wife’s wrongdoing and criminal acts.

Responding to the allegations, Safiqur Rahman’s lawyer, Arifur Rahman said, “The child gave a statement before the court. There, she said that she had never seen the MD. The MD himself did not beat her. Since the charge sheet has been filed, we will face the trial.”

What Bithi and Sufia Said

On 21 February, Bithi Akter, the wife of the former Biman MD, gave a confessional statement before Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Ismail. In her statement, she admitted to beating the child over three or four days but denied the allegations of severe torture.

Another domestic worker at the house, Sufia Begum, also gave a confessional statement before the court. She said the child had falsely accused her of stealing coconut oil and soap. For this reason, she admitted to beating the child for two days.

In her statement, Sufia said Bithi, the wife of the former Biman MD, would beat the child on various occasions, often in their presence.

She said, “One day, Madam told me to heat a spatula and bring it to her. I was working in the kitchen at the time. I did not take the spatula to her. Later, Madam came into the kitchen herself, heated the spatula and burnt the child’s left thigh with it.”

Sufia said she did not know why Bithi had burnt the child. She added that, after hearing the child scream, she went to her and applied cold water and cream to the girl’s thigh.

Father demands justice

Golam Mostafa, the complainant in the case and the child’s father, told Prothom Alo, “The scars on my daughter’s body are still there. Her eyes keep watering. I have enrolled her in a madrasah, but she has difficulty seeing.”

“I cannot afford my daughter’s medical treatment. I feel frightened when I see her scars. I want the harshest possible punishment for the accused so that no one else has to suffer such beatings,” Golam Mostafa said.

item.title: Dengue spreads along coast, but no special prevention plan in place
item.description:
The Mongla Upazila Health Complex in Bagerhat has 50 beds. On 18 October, 31 dengue patients were being treated there. So far this year, 532 dengue patients have been admitted to the facility.

Md Shaheen, the upazila health and family planning officer in Mongla, said the hospital never had so many dengue patients admitted before. He added that the number of hospital admissions did not fully reflect the severity of the outbreak. The situation was even worse, he said.

The situation in Mongla reflects the reality across the country’s coastal belt. Dengue was once largely confined to the capital, but it has now spread nationwide. However, the disease has spread more extensively in coastal areas. Nearly 40 per cnet of all dengue patients admitted to hospitals across Bangladesh this year have been in 19 coastal districts.

Since dengue re-emerged in the country in 2000, no other period has seen such a high proportion of hospital admissions in coastal districts.

The government has not provided any specific explanation for the high incidence of dengue in coastal areas. Researchers, entomologists, physicians and public health experts have offered several possible explanations.

Some of the factors, according to them, are coastal areas are relatively new transmission zones for dengue, known in epidemiology as “virgin areas”; water stored because of shortages of safe drinking water; poor sanitation and waterlogging in the absence of elected local government representatives; and natural breeding grounds in agricultural settings.

40pc of dengue patients in coastal districts

The spread of dengue beyond Dhaka and other major cities has been a subject of discussion for several years. District-level data from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) also show a rising number of cases in coastal districts.

The 19 coastal districts are Cox’s Bazar, Bagerhat, Barguna, Barishal, Bhola, Chandpur, Chattogram, Feni, Gopalganj, Jashore, Jhalakathi, Khulna, Lakshmipur, Narail, Noakhali, Pirojpur, Satkhira, Shariatpur and Patuakhali.

The survey noted that shortages of safe drinking water and limited access to deep groundwater had led local residents to store rainwater in drums. Stagnant water around homes and a lack of awareness about Aedes breeding sites could also be contributing to mosquito proliferation.

According to DGHS data, as many as 43,148 dengue patients had been admitted to hospitals in these 19 districts up to 17 October this year, accounting for 39.6 per cent of all hospitalised cases. During the same period, hospitals across the country saw an admission of a total of 110,312 dengue patients.

In 2023, hospitals in coastal areas admitted 97,552 dengue patients out of 321,179 cases nationwide, which was 30.4 per cent of the total.

In 2025, coastal districts recorded 35,511 hospital admissions, while the nationwide total was 102,358. The coastal share stood at around 34.7 per cent. However, the 2025 figures cover the entire year, whereas this year’s figures extend only to mid-October.

Public health expert Mushtuq Husain told Prothom Alo, “The figures we have for coastal areas are based on the locations of hospitals. They do not always tell us where patients live or where they contracted the infection. In reality, the number of cases in coastal areas is likely to be much higher.”

Why is dengue spreading so widely along the coast?

An analysis of data from Mongla Upazila Health Complex found that more than 55 per cent of its dengue patients came from Mongla municipality.

Upazila health officer Md Shaheen said coastal communities faced severe shortages of safe drinking water. Many people stored rainwater or other available water for later use. Since Aedes mosquitoes breed in clean water, he believed this was a major factor behind the outbreak in Mongla.

Waterlogging is also common in Mongla pourashava (municipality) and several union parishad headquarters because of inadequate drainage systems.

Shaheen said the pourashavas and union parishads currently had no elected representatives to oversee these issues. As a result, little was being done to address water that remained stagnant for long periods.

Dengue first emerged in Dhaka and gradually spread elsewhere. When transmission becomes widespread in one area, the virus finds new areas to spread to. Coastal regions offered favourable conditions for Aedes mosquitoes, which may explain the spread there, said entomologist Professor Kabirul Bashar.

Entomologist Kabirul Bashar The information we have about the relative contribution of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus to dengue transmission comes from experience in other countries. The situation in Bangladesh may be different. It is possible that Aedes albopictus has become a more significant carrier of the virus here. This requires detailed research.

In August this year, the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), under the DGHS, conducted a survey of Aedes mosquitoes in Barguna. Researchers examined 134 containers holding stagnant water at homes and other premises and found Aedes larvae in 26 of them.

The Breteau Index, which measures the number of containers containing Aedes larvae per 100 houses inspected, is an important indicator of mosquito infestation. A value above 20 is generally considered a sign of a serious situation. According to the survey, Barguna’s Breteau Index was 53.06.

The survey noted that shortages of safe drinking water and limited access to deep groundwater had led local residents to store rainwater in drums. Stagnant water around homes and a lack of awareness about Aedes breeding sites could also be contributing to mosquito proliferation.

Jannatul Ferdous, a senior scientific officer at IEDCR, told Prothom Alo that surveys had been conducted in Pirojpur as well as Barguna. Water shortages were a major factor, she said. However, Aedes mosquitoes were also found in large numbers in areca palm trunks and flower nurseries.

Unusually high presence of Aedes albopictus

There are two main types of Aedes mosquitoes that transmit dengue: Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. The former is responsible for most dengue transmission. Yet despite the high number of dengue cases along the coast, surveys have found a significant presence of Aedes albopictus in the region.

Professor Halimur Rashid, director of the disease control branch of the DGHSWork to prevent dengue is being carried out across the country. However, it is true that there is no special programme targeting coastal areas.

For instance, the IEDCR survey in Barguna in August found that nearly 58 per cent of the Aedes mosquitoes identified were Aedes albopictus, while 42 per cent were Aedes aegypti.

Globally, Aedes aegypti is estimated to account for around 95 per cent of dengue transmission by these two species, compared with just 5 per cent for Aedes albopictus. Why, then, is dengue spreading so extensively along the coast?

Responding to the question, entomologist Kabirul Bashar said, “The information we have about the relative contribution of Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus to dengue transmission comes from experience in other countries. The situation in Bangladesh may be different. It is possible that Aedes albopictus has become a more significant carrier of the virus here. This requires detailed research.”

Dengue deaths also higher in coastal areas this year

So far this year, dengue has claimed 342 lives across Bangladesh. Of these, 117 deaths were recorded in hospitals in the 19 coastal districts. The actual number could be higher, as not everyone who dies in a Dhaka hospital is a resident of the capital; some may come from coastal areas.

Even based on the 117 recorded deaths alone, the 19 coastal districts account for around 34 per cent of the national total.

Despite the rising dengue burden in this environmentally vulnerable region over the past several years, the government has no special plan targeting the coastal belt. Nor has there been a concerted effort to prevent the deaths occurring there.

Professor Halimur Rashid, director of the disease control branch of the DGHS, told Prothom Alo, “Work to prevent dengue is being carried out across the country. However, it is true that there is no special programme targeting coastal areas.”

Public health expert Mushtuq Hossain said, “Unfortunately, coastal areas have become major zones of infection over the past several years, yet I have not seen any specific plan for the region. The people of the coast are silent victims of the government’s overall indifference.”

item.title: Masked robbers hold over 100 passengers at gunpoint, loot 50–60 vehicles
item.description:
A group of robbers held passengers at gunpoint and looted their belongings in broad daylight on the Eidgaon–Eidgarh–Baishari road, which runs through the hilly areas of Eidgaon and Ramu upazilas in Cox’s Bazar. The incidents took place in two phases at Himchhari Dhala area on the road on Monday.

At least 50 to 60 vehicles, mostly CNG-run auto-rickshaws and motorcycles, fell victim to the robbers. More than 100 passengers were robbed of cash, mobile phones and other valuables.

Police had not arrested anyone in connection with the incidents by Monday evening.

According to the victims, an armed group of 10 to 12 masked men stopped vehicles on the road and held passengers at gunpoint. They then took them to the jungle nearby, beat them up and robbed them of money and belongings. Several victims alleged that the robberies continued for hours without any police patrol at the scene.

Confirming the incidents, Eidgaon police station officer-in-charge (OC) ATM Sifatul Majdar told Prothom Alo that some local criminals had set up roadblocks, robbed vehicles and taken shelter in the jungle.

Several police teams were conducting operations to detain them, but no one had been caught by the evening. Patrols had been stepped up in the dense forest areas along the 17-kilometre Eidgaon–Eidgarh–Baishari road. However, the OC could not confirm the total number of vehicles robbed.

Mohammad Robiul Islam, manager of the Eidgarh branch of a private organisation, said he was travelling by motorcycle from Eidgaon Bazar to Eidgarh with another person at around 12:00 pm on Monday. They were carrying Tk 120,000.

When they reached Himchhari Dhala, 10 to 12 masked and armed men stopped their motorcycle. The two men were then taken to a nearby jungle and beaten. The robbers searched them and snatched Tk 120,000, two mobile phones and documents before releasing them a short while later.

Robiul Islam said the robbers held more than 100 passengers travelling in 50 to 60 auto-rickshaws and motorcycles at gunpoint and looted them for nearly two hours. Police arrived at the scene and launched an operation at around 3:00 pm but failed to detain anyone. He also alleged that there had been no police patrol on the road during the incident.

Abdul Hakim, an accountant at the Eidgarh branch of another private organisation, said he and two others were travelling in an auto-rickshaw from Eidgaon Bazar to Eidgarh Bazar when armed robbers held them at gunpoint. They were taken to a jungle and beaten, and the robbers snatched Tk 150,000 and a bank cheque book.

Expressing his anger, Abdul Hakim said robberies occurred frequently on the road. Abductions for ransom were also common, yet no effective measures had been taken to ensure passengers’ safety.

Mohammad Tarek, a resident of Eidgarh, was also a victim of the robbery. He said he was travelling from Eidgaon to Eidgarh in a CNG-run auto-rickshaw with five passengers at around 6:30 am on Monday. When they reached Himchhari Dhala, the vehicle fell into the robbers’ hands. His mobile phone was taken, and he jumped out of the moving auto-rickshaw to escape with his life.

According to several people who were at the scene, the robberies took place in two phases, at 8:00 am and 12:00 pm on Monday. The two phases lasted around two and a half hours in total. They claimed that passengers in at least 50 to 60 vehicles fell victim to the robbers during that time.

item.title: PM leaves Dhaka to visit puja mandaps in three divisions
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Dhaka for Rangpur Tuesday morning to visit Durga Puja mandaps in three divisions-Rangpur, Rajshahi and Chattogram on Maha Navami, the ninth day of the Hindu community's biggest religious festival, Durga Puja.

He departed Tejgaon Airport aboard a military aircraft for Saidpur Airport in Nilphamari at 9:00 am, Prime Minister's Press Secretary AAM Saleh Shibly said.

In Rangpur, the prime minister is scheduled to visit the puja mandap at Radha Gobinda Temple and exchange greetings with devotees before proceeding to Rajshahi and Chattogram, returning to Dhaka tonight.

According to the schedule, he will depart Saidpur Airport for Rajshahi's Shah Makhdum Airport at 12:30 pm and visit the puja mandap at Dharmasabha Temple at 1:15 pm.

After a brief stop at Rajshahi Circuit House at 2:15 pm, he will attend a public meeting at the playground of Haji Muhammad Mohsin Government High School at 3:00 pm.

The prime minister will leave Shah Makhdum Airport for Chattogram's Shah Amanat International Airport at 4:15 pm and visit the puja mandap at JM Sen Hall in Rahmatganj at 5:30 pm.

Opposition paving way for autocracy would betray July, Liberation War martyrs: PM

After a brief stop at Chattogram Circuit House at 6:45 pm, he is scheduled to depart for Dhaka at 7:45 pm, arriving at Tejgaon Airport at 9:15 pm.

"The government's policy is that religion belongs to individuals, while everyone has the right to security," Shibly quoted the prime minister as saying.

He said the government had taken all necessary measures to ensure the smooth celebration of Durga Puja by the Hindu community across the country, including increased allocations, extended holidays and support for puja mandaps.

The prime minister is accompanied by BNP Standing Committee Member Gayeshwar Chandra Roy, Women and Children Affairs Minister Prof AZM Zahid Hossain, BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi, Cultural Affairs Minister Nitai Roy Chowdhury, State Minister for LGRD and Cooperatives Mir Shahe Alam, Prime Minister's Adviser Rehan Asif Asad, PM's Special Assistant Bijon Kanti Sarker and BNP Special Secretary Belayet Hossain Mridha, among others.

Earlier, the prime minister visited puja mandaps in Dhaka's Mohakhali and Banani areas, accompanied by his wife Zubaida Rahman.

Maha Navami, the penultimate major day of Durga Puja celebrations, falls today. The festival will conclude tomorrow with the immersion of idols.

item.title: Bangladesh awaits verdict copy on execution of 2 nationals in Saudi: Shama
item.description:
Amid concern over the execution of two Bangladeshis in the Saudi Arabia without prior communication, Dhaka on Monday said the government is still waiting for a copy of the verdict from the Saudi authorities to know the details.

Bangladesh has also sought an explanation from its friendly bilateral partner, citing a possible gap in information sharing and communication between the two countries.

It expects foreign countries to notify it when Bangladeshi nationals face criminal proceedings abroad so that consular access can be provided to them.

State Minister-1 for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and State Minister-2 Shama Obaed Islam briefed newspersons separately at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions,” said State Minister Kobir, describing the execution of two Bangladeshis as “very disappointing.”

The state minister, however, said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman and his government enjoy good and deep relations with the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, expressing hope that the ties would reach a new height. He said there appeared to have been a lapse somewhere in the process.

Talking to newspersons separately, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed said they are still waiting for a copy of the verdict to know the details.

“Please wait until we know what the verdict says. After that, we will discuss the matter with the Saudi authorities and explore what can be done,” she said, noting that the government is awaiting detailed information from Saudi Arabia.

“Periodically, they provide us with a list, and we officially come to know through such a list how many people have been arrested and when. We are checking the list to see whether their names are included,” Shama said.

She said the government is yet to receive detailed information about the individuals concerned and formally sought further details from the Saudi authorities.

“As of now, we do not have any additional information. We have sought detailed information from them. Once they provide it, we may have a clearer picture of the situation,” Shama said.

Regarding Bangladeshis who die abroad, she said the government tries its best to communicate with their families and provide the necessary assistance.

Citing an incident in Saudi Arabia in 2023, she said the government had ensured compensation for the two children of a Bangladeshi who was killed there, and the family received the compensation on Monday.

She said legal procedures varied from country to country, adding that Saudi Arabia has its own legal framework.

State Minister Kobir said Bangladesh would inform the Saudi authorities if a Saudi national was arrested here on a criminal charge, enabling them to provide consular access.

“At the very least, they should know that one of their citizens has become involved in criminal activities on Bangladeshi soil,” he said.

Bangladesh expected similar communication from Saudi Arabia and other countries so that it could extend assistance to its nationals, he added.

Kobir said Saudi Arabia had its own laws and that anyone travelling there was subject to those laws.

He also said involvement in criminal activities by anyone at a sacred site visited by people for religious purposes is unacceptable.

BBC, the world’s leading public service broadcaster, quoting the Saudi interior ministry, said the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under “tazir”, which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.

The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the “sanctity” of the mosque, reports BBC.

Saudi envoy’s talks with MoFA

Bangladesh on Sunday sought further information from Saudi Arabia regarding the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, raising the issue with Saudi Ambassador to Bangladesh, Abdullah Zafer bin Abiyah.

Secretary (East & West) Md Nazrul Islam sought detailed information about the executions during a meeting with the Saudi Ambassador, a senior official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs told UNB.

When asked whether the move could be described as a summons, another official told UNB, “No, it was not.”

Although Dhaka raised the issue with the Saudi envoy, it expressed confidence that the incident would not affect the strong bilateral relations between the two countries.

The importance of staying “mindful” of the laws of the host country was also discussed.

Both sides expressed satisfaction with the steady progress of cooperation between Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia across various sectors.

Earlier, Saudi media reported that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia had executed the two Bangladeshis after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque in the holy city of Mecca.

Quoting the Saudi Interior Ministry, Gulf News reported that the court imposed the sentences because of the seriousness of the offence, the violation of the sanctity of the mosque, and the circumstances in which the acts were committed.

The Saudi authorities identified the two Bangladeshis as Nazrul Islam Abdul Basir and Sweety Akhtar.

“On 14 October, we learned that two Bangladeshi nationals had been sentenced to death under Saudi Arabian law and that the executions had been carried out,” State Minister Shama Obaed Islam said, noting that neither the Ministry of Foreign Affairs nor the Bangladesh Mission in Saudi Arabia had been informed in advance.

“We wanted to know whatever we needed to know. Let the reply come. I will be able to let you know,” Shama said.

Upon learning of the incident, the Bangladesh Mission notified the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment, sharing all the information it had gathered from the Saudi authorities.

The state minister also said the government had sent a formal inquiry to ascertain the full details, including the identities of the individuals, their backgrounds in Bangladesh, and when they had originally arrived in Saudi Arabia for work.

Based on past experience, the state minister said Saudi Arabia had its own legal framework and that anyone found guilty of a grave offence was punished in accordance with the country’s laws.

“The execution of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia serves as a major lesson for us,” she said.

Shama further said the repatriation of the bodies could be arranged once a response to the letter was received from Saudi Arabia.

Kobir’s engagements in Baku, Bagdad

Briefing journalists on his overseas visit, Humaiun Kobir said he had attended the CICA summit in Baku, Azerbaijan, before travelling to Baghdad to attend the OIC Council of Foreign Ministers’ meeting.

He described the visit as productive and said international stakeholders showed considerable interest in Bangladesh during meetings held on the sidelines.

At the OIC meeting, he made a strong appeal on behalf of the government for member states to come forward and help resolve the Rohingya crisis.

Kobir also co-chaired an ad hoc ministerial meeting on Rohingya accountability with the Foreign Minister of The Gambia.

He said the discussions prioritised the Rohingya issue and explored how OIC member states could work together to promote peace.

Asked about discussions on a possible Bangladeshi role in maintaining stability in the Middle East, drawing on the country’s peacekeeping experience, he said no substantive discussions took place during the visit on Bangladesh’s participation in any specific initiative.

item.title: Dhaka seeks to know whether the 2 Bangladeshis had a chance to defend themselves
item.description:
The names of Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter appeared on a list of detainees sent by Saudi Arabia to Bangladesh. Although offences against them were mentioned, the list did not specify their sentences. Later, both were executed. Dhaka has asked Riyadh why Bangladesh was not informed about the death sentences.

Bangladesh’s Consul General, Md Sakhawat Hossain, raised the question at a meeting on Monday in Jeddah with Farid bin Saad Al Shehri, director general of Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs. According to several officials at Bangladesh’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Saudi official was unable to provide a satisfactory answer.

Bangladesh sent another diplomatic note to Saudi Arabia the same day, seeking details of the cases and the judicial proceedings involving the two Bangladeshis. It also asked whether they had been given an opportunity to defend themselves.

Sakhawat Hossain confirmed to Prothom Alo that the meeting had taken place and that another diplomatic note had been sent. He, however, declined to disclose details of the discussions.

After son’s execution in Saudi Arabia, parents want to see his body just once

Several officials at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs told Prothom Alo on Monday evening that, during the meeting in Jeddah, Bangladesh’s consul general asked why information about the sentences had been omitted from the regularly supplied list of detainees, despite the inclusion of the two individuals’ names.

A senior ministry official told Prothom Alo that the latest diplomatic note sought detailed accounts of the cases involving the two Bangladeshis who had been executed, the various steps taken during the judicial proceedings, and whether they had been given any opportunity to defend themselves after being convicted.

Death sentence for two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia a lesson for us: Shama Obaed

On 14 October, the Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the Saudi Ministry of Interior, reported that the two Bangladeshis had been executed. The following day, on 15 October, the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah sent a diplomatic note to the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs seeking details about the two citizens who had been sentenced to death. The note was sent again to the Saudi ambassador in Dhaka on 18 October.

Bangladeshi officials said that, during Monday’s discussions in Jeddah, they requested that detailed information about the two executed Bangladeshis be provided as soon as possible. The meeting took place in a cordial atmosphere.

The Saudi side said that, following their arrests in August 2023, the two defendants had initially been sentenced by a lower court after due judicial process. An appellate court panel comprising 13 judges later upheld their death sentences. The executions were carried out in separate cells designated for men and women, in accordance with the court’s verdicts.

During the meeting, Bangladesh’s consul general also raised discrepancies in the list supplied by Saudi Arabia. In particular, he asked why the list sent to Bangladesh omitted the sentences imposed on Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter if their trials had been conducted in accordance with due process.

The Bangladeshi diplomat also said that, had the Jeddah mission learned from the list that the two had been sentenced to death, it could have taken steps to protect them. The Saudi diplomat was unable to provide a satisfactory answer to this question.

2 Bangladeshis executed in Mecca, Govt seeks details from Saudi ambassador

Both worked for the same company

Sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that, on 30 September, the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a list of convicted individuals to the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah. The names of Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akter appeared on it. They were from Brahmanbaria and Tangail districts, respectively. After arriving in Saudi Arabia in late 2022, both joined Al Majal Company as cleaners.

Both convicted on separate charges

Information obtained from Bangladeshi diplomats in Dhaka, Riyadh and Jeddah, along with several official documents, shows that Nazrul Islam was detained on 1 August 2023 and Sweety Akter the following day, on 2 August.

The list sent on 30 September stated that Nazrul Islam, who was being held at Jeddah Correctional Facility, had been convicted of cybercrime or an offence related to information technology. However, the list did not specify when he had been sentenced or what punishment had been imposed.

The list identified Sweety Akter as being held at Jeddah Women’s Prison. It mentioned a charge of adultery against her but provided no details of her sentence.

A message sent by the Bangladesh mission in Jeddah to Dhaka on 18 October stated that there was no known precedent for a Bangladeshi citizen being sentenced to death in the oil-rich country for cybercrime or adultery.

The message also said that 306 Bangladeshis were being held in prisons in western Saudi Arabia in connection with various cases involving moral turpitude. Of them, 147 had been sentenced to terms ranging from one month to 15 years in prison. In addition, three Bangladeshis had been sentenced in three separate cybercrime cases in Mecca, receiving prison terms ranging from six months to five years.

Executions of two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia disappointing for us: Humaiun Kobir

‘The matter is disappointing’

Foreign Affairs State Minister Humaiun Kobir spoke to journalists at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday afternoon about the executions of the two Bangladeshis.

He said, “The fact that the execution was carried out after allegations or criminal offences (brought against the two Bangladeshis in Saudi Arabia) is disappointing for us.”

Responding to journalists’ questions about the recent executions of the two Bangladeshi citizens in Saudi Arabia, the state minister said there had been lapses in information-sharing and diplomatic communication.

He also said the Saudi authorities had been asked to provide a detailed explanation of the incident and relevant information.

item.title: Ronaldo handed 30-day suspension after walking out on Portugal
item.description:
FILES-FBL-POR-RONALDO

Cristiano Ronaldo has been handed a 30-day suspension for leaving the Portuguese national team camp, the country's football federation (FPF) announced on Monday.

The 41-year-old abruptly left the Portugal camp on 30 September during the UEFA Nations League, before accusing coach Jorge Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time.

Ronaldo apologised to supporters earlier in October, adding he would accept any punishment that was imposed.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid star, who will also have to pay a fine of 255 euros ($286), has received the minimum penalty provided for in the federation's regulations, which stipulate suspensions of between one and six months for leaving the national team.

Ronaldo left Portugal's squad after first being made to warm up as a substitute against Norway on 27 September and not being brought on, and then finding out he would not start against Denmark in the match on 1 October.

Ronaldo's suspension takes effect from the day of the Denmark match, meaning he has already served 19 days of his ban and will complete it by the end of October.

The FPF disciplinary committee said it took into account "the remorse shown in the statement" issued by Ronaldo on 6 October, in which he admitted his mistake and expressed his willingness to accept a punishment.

The five-time Ballon d'Or winner is Portugal's all-time top goalscorer and record appearance-maker in men's international football.

But in his absence, Portugal won all four of their Nations League matches and qualified for the quarter-finals with two games to spare.

Portugal host Denmark on 14 November and then travel to face Wales on 17 November in their final two Nations League Group A4 matches -- by which time Ronaldo will have served his suspension.

“Putting in the work”

In a social media post shortly after his walk-out, Ronaldo accused Portugal boss Jesus of breaking his word about giving him game time in Nations League matches but insisted he was not retiring from international duty.

"I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team," Ronaldo posted.

He said Jesus had gone back on his word about bringing him on against Norway, and then in a press conference before the Denmark match had not said a series of points they had agreed upon during a conversation beforehand.

One of Ronaldo's pre-approved talking points was that Jesus had "made a mistake in asking someone of the stature of Pele or Maradona to warm up and then not sending him on in the match".

Jesus, speaking several days later, said he would select Ronaldo for international duty if the forward was playing for his club Al Nassr, and was interested in being called up.

Following the FPF's announcement, Ronaldo did not directly react to the news on Instagram but did post a picture of himself preparing to train with his Saudi club, accompanied with the caption, "Putting in the work".

item.title: PSC to end ‘repeat cadre’ appointments changes may begin with 50th BCS
item.description:
The Bangladesh Public Service Commission (BPSC) has taken steps to address the problem of candidates receiving repeated recommendations for the same cadre post in the Bangladesh Civil Service (BCS) examinations, leaving valuable cadre positions vacant as a result.

Since taking office, the commission’s new chairman has issued specific instructions and launched initiatives to tackle the issue.

According to commission sources, the issue of repeat cadre appointments will receive particular attention when the final results of the upcoming 50th BCS examination are published.

In the BCS recruitment process, the term 'repeat cadre' primarily refers to candidates who, despite having already received a recommendation or secured final appointment to a particular cadre in an earlier BCS examination (such as the administration, police or education cadre) receive another recommendation for the same cadre in a subsequent examination.

As a result, these candidates do not take up the same position again, leaving valuable civil service posts vacant. Other jobseekers ultimately bear the cost of this practice.

Owing to these prolonged delays and inconsistencies, hundreds of qualified and talented candidates miss out on cadre appointments every year.

51st BCS: Applications open, what you need to know

'Repeat cadre' issue under scrutiny, 44th BCS highlights the problem

The inconsistency surrounding repeat cadre appointments in BCS recruitment examinations has persisted for years.

However, the issue sparked considerable discussion and controversy following the publication of the 43rd BCS results and, in particular, the final results of the 44th BCS examination.

An analysis of data provided by the BPSC shows that, when the commission recommended 1,710 candidates against 1,710 vacant posts in the 44th BCS, nearly 400 of those selected were repeat cadre candidates.

In other words, they already held positions in various government cadres, and had received recommendations for the same cadre again. The presence of nearly 400 repeat cadre candidates in a single BCS examination posed a major administrative challenge for both the BPSC and the Ministry of Public Administration.

Following the incident, strong demands emerged for the commission to fill the posts associated with repeat cadre candidates by selecting new candidates from the waiting list according to merit.

50th BCS results to reflect actual vacancies

Although the authorities have previously amended the BCS rules to prevent repeat cadre appointments, the problem remains unresolved.

In many cases, candidates who qualify in two BCS examinations withhold information and secure another appointment to the same cadre, allowing the complication to persist. The commission is therefore taking practical measures to address the issue rather than relying solely on provisions on paper.

The final gazette notification for the 45th BCS has already been published, and the authorities have scheduled 1 November as the date for the recommended candidates to join their new posts.

Only after the candidates join their respective cadre positions will the authorities be able to determine how many actually take up their posts and how many vacancies remain.

According to BPSC sources, the exact number of candidates who have joined will be monitored after 1 November. It will then prepare the final recommendations for the 50th BCS based on verified vacancy figures, ensuring that new candidates can be appointed to the posts that remain vacant.

General jobseekers have welcomed the commission’s practical approach. Mizanur Rahman, a BCS candidate, told Prothom Alo, "Candidates like us face severe discrimination because of repeat cadre appointments. One person repeatedly sits the examinations while withholding information and occupies the same position, yet the post ultimately remains vacant."

"If the BPSC finalises its recommendations for the 50th BCS based on accurate figures for candidates joining the 45th BCS, the problem of vacant posts will be significantly reduced," he added.

51st special BCS circular issued with 5,000 posts, when will general BCS be held?

In this regard, SM Matiur Rahman, the BPSC’s public relations officer, told Prothom Alo that the repeat cadre problem deprives countless qualified candidates of opportunities they deserve every year. He said the commission’s new chairman had made eliminating this inconsistency a top priority since taking office.

The commission will review the precise figures for candidates joining the 45th BCS on 1 November and incorporate them into the 50th BCS results, ensuring that no posts remain vacant and that deserving candidates receive their rightful opportunities.

Following the complications involving repeat cadre appointments in the 44th BCS, the BPSC took steps to amend the recruitment rules and submitted a proposal to the Ministry of Public Administration.

The proposed provision states that, while preparing the final results or submitting the final recommendations to the government, the commission may refrain from recommending a candidate again if it has information that the candidate is being nominated for the same cadre post or an equivalent position and is unwilling to join.

The proposal also allows the commission to select candidates further down the merit list to fill those vacant posts and publish a “supplementary result”.

item.title: Natore road accident: Bus supervisor was driving while driver slept in rear seat
item.description:
Sohel Rana, the supervisor of an RP Special Paribahan bus, was driving when the vehicle met with an accident in Bonpara, Natore. The driver and his assistant were sleeping in the rear seats at the time, according to three passengers on the bus.

Sohel Rana, 38, was from Faradpur village in Godagari upazila of Rajshahi. He is survived by his wife and two children. His family members said he had previously worked as a bus driver but began working as a bus supervisor about two years ago.

Fourteen people were killed and at least 32 injured when an RP Special Paribahan bus collided with a sand-laden truck on the Natore-Pabna highway in Bonpara, Baraigram upazila, Natore, at around 4am on Tuesday.

Ramzan Ali, 28, from Gomostapur upazila in Chapainawabganj, was a passenger on the bus. He was injured in the accident and received treatment at Bonpara Patwari Hospital. He left the hospital at around 8:30am for further treatment.

Speaking to Prothom Alo, he said, “I was sitting two seats behind the driver. When the bus reached Ishwardi in Pabna at around 3am, the driver got up from his seat and the supervisor began driving. The driver closed the bus door, and he and his assistant went to sleep in the rear seats. About an hour later, when the bus reached Bonpara, it collided head-on with a truck coming from the opposite direction.”

Two other passengers, Yakub Ali and Abdus Salam, were injured and received treatment at Bonpara Patwari Hospital. While undergoing treatment, they said the supervisor was driving the bus at the time of the accident, while the driver and his helper were sitting in the rear seats.

The bus had departed from Barguna district town at around 7pm on Monday. After a brief stop in Ishwardi, the bus resumed its journey with the supervisor at the wheel. The accident occurred a short time later.

Sohel Rana’s body arrived at his home in Faradpur village around noon on Tuesday. At the house, family members and relatives were seen grieving, while neighbours and local residents gathered there.

Sohel Rana’s wife, Dolly Begum, said her husband had previously driven buses but began working as a supervisor about two years ago.

Asked about who was driving the bus involved in the accident, Sub-Inspector Alamgir Hossain of Bonpara Highway Police Station said the incident would be investigated and nothing can be said with certainty before the investigation.

item.title: "Perhaps he did it with good intentions" - Jamaat Ameer on Ishraque’s display of weapons
item.description:
Commenting on Ishraque Hossain’s resignation from the post of State Minister for Liberation War Affairs, Shafiqur Rahman, Ameer of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami and Leader of the Opposition in Parliament, said, “There is no scope for anyone to describe his actions negatively. However, if an elected representative and a state minister openly carries a firearm in broad daylight or points it at someone, he may have done so with good intentions. But there is no shortage of people in this society who might use it with bad intentions. They will use this as a reference. If you look at the matter from the perspective of civil conduct, that is the only point of objection. There is nothing to object to about his actions otherwise.”

Shafiqur Rahman made these remarks on Tuesday while answering journalists’ questions after a conference of former party associates and members organised by Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami’s Chattogram city unit at the GEC Convention Centre in Chattogram. He had earlier attended the conference as the chief guest. When asked about the role of the police, he said, “Ishraque has already said that on my behalf.”

Earlier, Ishraque Hossain came under controversy after taking part in an anti-drug operation in the capital’s Gandaria area last Saturday while carrying a firearm. He later stepped down as State Minister for Liberation War Affairs. Saying that he had resigned at the Prime Minister’s direction, Ishraque said he had taken the decision to spare the BNP and the government from an “embarrassing” situation. However, he also maintained that he had done nothing wrong during the operation.

Commenting on the resignation, Shafiqur Rahman said, “Look, this was a matter of an internal party decision on their (BNP’s) part. Subsequently, a decision was made, and it was said that the Prime Minister had wanted this, which is why he resigned. Drugs are destroying society. He [Ishraque] has said that the police and other forces were present there. It would have been better if he had not been carrying a firearm. That is all.”

Earlier, addressing the conference of former party associates and members as the chief guest, Shafiqur Rahman said that students and the public had not shed blood in July for looters and extortionists. The people would never accept looting, extortion, or injustice and oppression under any circumstances. In the future, those responsible would have to account for every crime. Anyone who oppresses people, deprives them of their rights, or usurps what rightfully belongs to others would have to be held accountable.

The conference was chaired by Muhammad Nazrul Islam, Ameer of Jamaat-e-Islami’s Chattogram city unit. Special guests included Nurul Islam, central president of Bangladesh Islami Chhatra Shibir; Jamaat’s Assistant Secretaries-General AHM Hamidur Rahman Azad and Muhammad Shahjahan; Nurul Islam, Ameer of Jamaat’s Dhaka South city unit and a Member of Parliament; Muhammad Selim Uddin, Ameer of Jamaat’s Dhaka North city unit; Shahjahan Chowdhury, a member of the central executive council and a Member of Parliament; Jasim Uddin Sarkar, former vice-president of Chittagong University Central Students’ union (CUCSU); and SM Farhad, general secretary of Dhaka University Central Students’ union (DUCSU).

item.title: Bangladesh’s hidden climate bill: How much are we losing?
item.description:
Bangladesh has earned global recognition for reducing deaths from cyclones and floods. Early warning systems, cyclone shelters, embankments and community preparedness have transformed the country’s disaster response. Yet another climate crisis is receiving far less attention: the economic damage climate change is quietly inflicting on households, farmers, workers, businesses and public finances.

The question is no longer whether climate change is costing Bangladesh. It clearly is. The real question is how much we are losing, who is paying the price and whether the country is doing enough to prevent these losses.
The uncomfortable reality is that Bangladesh still lacks a comprehensive annual system for calculating climate induced microeconomic damage. Losses are recorded separately through agricultural damage, disaster assessments, health costs, infrastructure destruction, lost working days, business interruption, declining household income and climate induced migration. As a result, much of the country’s real climate bill remains invisible.

Available evidence shows that the cost is already enormous. The World Bank estimates that tropical cyclones cost Bangladesh around US$1 billion annually. It has also warned that a severe flood could reduce national GDP by as much as 9 per cent, while climate change could cause around one third of agricultural GDP to be lost by 2050. As many as 13.3 million people could become internal climate migrants by 2050 because of climate related pressures on agriculture, water and land. The economic burden is no longer limited to cyclones and floods.

Extreme heat is emerging as a major source of economic loss. A 2025 World Bank assessment found that heat related physical and mental health conditions resulted in an estimated 250 million lost workdays in Bangladesh in 2024. The resulting economic loss was estimated at between US$1.33 billion and US$1.78 billion, equivalent to around 0.3 to 0.4 per cent of GDP.

The invisible cost of climate change: Bangladesh's non-economic losses

This should fundamentally change how Bangladesh understands climate damage. A disaster does not have to destroy a house, factory or bridge to cause economic loss. When extreme heat reduces the productivity of a construction worker, garment worker, farmer, transport worker or street vendor, the economy loses output.

The hidden climate bill therefore extends far beyond physical destruction.
Consider a farmer in coastal Bangladesh. Rising salinity may gradually reduce agricultural production. The immediate result is lower household income. But the consequences do not end there. A family may sell livestock, borrow money, reduce food consumption or withdraw children from school. Eventually, one or more family members may migrate to Dhaka or another city.

A climate shock that begins in a field can therefore become a problem for the labour market, housing, education, health services and urban infrastructure.

The same chain of losses occurs during floods. A small shopkeeper can lose inventory. A transport worker can lose several days of income. A factory may remain physically undamaged but stop production because roads are submerged or workers cannot reach their workplace.

Households may spend their savings on repairs instead of education, healthcare or investment. At the same time, the government must spend more on emergency relief, damaged roads, embankment repair, reconstruction and public health.

Climate change therefore creates a double burden: private income and productive assets are lost while public expenditure increases.

This is why Bangladesh urgently needs a national climate loss accounting system. It should systematically measure household and productive asset losses, agricultural and fisheries damage, lost income and working days, health and productivity costs, business interruption, supply chain disruption, displacement and loss of human capital.

Such a system would tell policymakers not simply how much a cyclone or flood costs in physical damage, but how much income ordinary citizens lose and how much economic activity Bangladesh sacrifices.

This is particularly important because a large share of Bangladesh’s workers remain in informal employment. Agricultural labourers, construction workers, transport workers, street vendors and small entrepreneurs often have limited access to paid leave, insurance or social protection. When a flood, cyclone or heatwave prevents them from working, their income can disappear immediately. Climate change is therefore also an inequality crisis.

A wealthier household may be able to repair its home, relocate temporarily or pay medical expenses. A poor household may have to sell productive assets or take on debt. For families living close to the poverty line, one climate shock can erase years of economic progress.

Bangladesh has taken important steps toward adaptation. Its National Adaptation Plan for 2023 to 2050 identifies major adaptation priorities and recognises the enormous investment required to protect people, livelihoods and development. But the gap between ambition and implementation remains a serious concern.

The first major gap is data. Bangladesh cannot effectively manage climate related economic damage without knowing its full scale. The government should publish an annual National Climate Economic Loss Report covering households, agriculture, businesses, labour productivity, health and public infrastructure.

The second gap is institutional coordination. Climate adaptation cannot remain primarily the responsibility of environmental or disaster management agencies. Climate risks must be integrated into agriculture, finance, labour, health, housing, transport, industry, education and urban planning.

The third gap is prevention. Bangladesh has become relatively successful at responding after disasters, but prevention deserves much greater economic priority. A resilient drainage system that prevents repeated business disruption may be more valuable than repeatedly repairing flood damage. A climate resilient crop can protect rural income for years. A heat resilient workplace can preserve thousands of working days.

The fourth challenge is finance. Bangladesh cannot meet its enormous adaptation needs through public budgets alone. International climate finance, concessional financing, private investment, insurance and innovative financial mechanisms will all be necessary.

International experience offers useful lessons. The Netherlands demonstrates how flood protection can be integrated into long term spatial planning, infrastructure and water management. Its experience shows that flood resilience can be treated as an economic strategy rather than simply an emergency response.

Singapore offers another important lesson, particularly for Bangladesh’s cities. Its approach to rising temperatures combines urban greenery, heat modelling, climate sensitive planning and protection of vulnerable populations. Dhaka could similarly treat trees, shaded public spaces, cool buildings, drainage and water management as economic infrastructure rather than merely environmental amenities.

Bangladesh can also build on its own success. Its cyclone warning system and community preparedness programmes demonstrate that locally rooted approaches can deliver remarkable results. The same principle should now be applied to protecting livelihoods, small businesses, agriculture and workers.

Most importantly, adaptation should be judged by economic outcomes. Instead of simply reporting how much money is spent on a climate project, the government should measure how many jobs are protected, how much income is safeguarded, how many working days are preserved and how much future economic loss is avoided.

The real climate bill is not simply the cost of rebuilding a bridge after a flood. It is the farmer who produces less for years because of salinity. It is the worker who loses productive days because of extreme heat. It is the small entrepreneur whose capital disappears in a flood. It is the child whose education is interrupted because household income collapses. It is the family forced to migrate after losing its land.

When millions of such individual losses accumulate, they become a national economic crisis. Bangladesh has demonstrated that it can protect its people from the deadliest consequences of climate disasters. The next challenge is to protect their livelihoods and economic future.

The country cannot manage what it does not measure. It is time to move from simply counting disasters to counting lost income, lost jobs, lost working days, damaged productive assets and the GDP that climate change prevents Bangladesh from generating.

The objective should not simply be to calculate how much climate change costs Bangladesh. It should be to determine how much Bangladesh can save by investing in resilience today.

Climate adaptation is no longer merely an environmental responsibility. For Bangladesh, it is an investment in GDP, employment, poverty reduction, human development and long term economic security. The climate bill is already being paid. The failure is that we still do not know its full size.

* The writer is the Editor and CSO of News Network

item.title: 14 years of misery, Tk 30b spent, only for the project to be cancelled
item.description:
Construction continued for 14 years, costing Tk 28.11 billion (2,811 crore). Yet the special buses for which the project was undertaken never began operating.

Instead, traffic congestion and public suffering increased along the 20-kilometre stretch of the Dhaka–Mymensingh Highway between the airport and Gazipur. The government has now decided to cancel the project and convert the existing infrastructure into a conventional highway.

At a cabinet meeting chaired by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday, the government discussed the future of the Gazipur Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project. The Road Transport and Highways Division issued a letter the following day outlining the discussions and decisions taken at the meeting.

Under the decision, the government has proposed removing the BRT corridor’s stations and lane dividers and converting the road into a conventional highway with three to six lanes. It has also proposed upgrading two two-lane flyovers to four lanes.

The authorities have been instructed to consult the relevant development partners, resolve legal complications and take the necessary steps to close the project.

The cabinet has also approved a proposal to shut down the Dhaka Bus Rapid Transit Company, established to operate the BRT service, and transfer its functions to the Roads and Highways Department (RHD).

The government has directed the relevant authorities to take urgent action to implement the cabinet’s decisions. They must report progress to the ministry within 15 days and submit further progress reports by the third day of every month until the process is complete.

According to sources at the Road Transport and Highways Division, the cabinet discussed four alternatives: (1) cancelling the project; (2) completing the unfinished work, procuring BRT buses and launching the service; (3) retaining the BRT corridor in its existing condition and allowing both dedicated buses and existing private buses to operate; and (4) operating the BRT corridor as a toll road.

The government ultimately decided to cancel the project and use the road as a conventional highway. This means the existing stations and the dividers separating the BRT lanes will have to be demolished. The flyovers will be expanded in the future.

However, an organisation called Gazipur Heritage and Development has been campaigning for the completion of the BRT project and the introduction of dedicated buses. It has held several press conferences in support of the project and sent letters to various government offices.

Mohammad Shamsul Haque, president of the organisation, told Prothom Alo on Tuesday that residents of Gazipur had endured unimaginable suffering over the past 14 years. He argued that cancelling the project after 97 per cent of the work had been completed would be wrong. He said the organisation would send a letter protesting the government’s decision.

Experts support cancelling the project

Before the government decided the future of the BRT project, an expert team from Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET) reviewed its technical aspects.

Professor Shamsul Haque of BUET’s Department of Civil Engineering led the team. The experts submitted their report to the Road Transport and Highways Division in October last year.

After reviewing reports from two committees formed by the Road Transport and Highways Division during the interim government’s tenure, the BUET team recommended cancelling the project entirely and upgrading the existing infrastructure for use as an improved highway.

The report described the project as an example of “systemic failure” in the planning and implementation of infrastructure projects in Bangladesh. The team attributed the situation to inadequate technical assessments, a shortage of skilled personnel and a lack of accountability. It also identified flaws in the project’s planning and design, along with poor coordination among the agencies involved.

According to sources at the Road Transport and Highways Division, the government had planned to build another BRT corridor from Uttara to Keraniganj with funding from the World Bank.

However, the second project was cancelled because the Gazipur–Airport corridor failed to begin operations on time. This raised questions about the viability of the Gazipur–Airport section.

Another challenge concerns the doors of buses currently operating in Bangladesh, which are located on the left-hand side. The BRT stations, however, have been designed for buses with doors on the right-hand side.

Although right-side doors are standard for BRT systems worldwide, buses with this configuration would not be able to operate beyond the Gazipur–Airport corridor.

Professor Shamsul Haque, head of the BUET expert team, told Prothom Alo that cancelling the project was the best option among the possible alternatives.

However, he emphasised that the people of Gazipur and others travelling along the route had endured hardship for 14 years and deserved an alternative transport arrangement.

He explained that, even if the BRT buses began operating, residents of Gazipur would only be able to travel as far as the airport and would then have to change buses, making the system impractical.

Shamsul Haque added that cancelling the project and converting the corridor into a high-speed highway would benefit users of Gazipur’s industrial areas. He also suggested introducing commuter train services from Gazipur to Kamalapur, noting that construction of the railway’s third and fourth lines was nearing completion.

Project costs more than tripled                    

The ousted Awami League government launched the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) project in 2012 to connect the airport with Shibbari in Gazipur, covering approximately 20 kilometres. Of the total route, 15.07 kilometres consists of road-level sections, with the remainder running on elevated structures.

The plan was to operate dedicated buses along two separate lanes in the middle of the road. Officials projected that the service would carry around 25,000 passengers a day once operational. The buses were expected to avoid traffic congestion, traffic signals and other obstructions.

The BRT project relied primarily on foreign funding. Alongside the Asian Development Bank (ADB), the French Development Agency (AFD) and the Global Environment Facility (GEF) are financing the project.

The initial estimated cost stood at around Tk 20.40 billion (2,040 crore). The authorities planned to complete construction in 2016 and introduce special buses with automatic doors in 2017.

However, construction never finished. Three revisions pushed the estimated cost up to Tk 42.68 billion (4,268 crore), of which Tk 28.11 billion (2,811 crore) has been spent.

In 2025, the authorities proposed a fourth revision, which would have increased the project cost to Tk 65.98 billion (6,598 crore) and extended the deadline to 2029. However, during the interim government’s tenure, the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC) did not approve the revised proposal. Instead, it instructed the authorities to explore alternatives and identify the individuals or organisations responsible for the design flaws.

Although Bangladesh’s BRT project was the country’s first, many other countries already operate such systems. According to the website Global BRT Data, 191 cities worldwide have BRT systems, carrying more than 32.5 million passengers daily.

Neighbouring India operates BRT systems in 13 cities. These systems, spanning 228 kilometres, carry around 500,000 passengers a day. China’s BRT systems carry approximately 4.4 million passengers daily, while Taiwan’s systems serve around 1.35 million.

Unfinished infrastructure adds to public suffering

Authorities have built infrastructure for 15 stations along the middle of the road between the airport and Gazipur. However, none of the stations is fully complete.

Several pedestrian overbridges designed to help passengers board and leave buses have escalators and lifts, but many of these facilities remain unusable. Equipment has rusted in some places, while structures are deteriorating elsewhere.

The authorities installed concrete barriers along the centre of the road to separate the BRT lanes, with metal fencing at certain points. These structures have reduced the space available for other traffic. Vehicles also face difficulties where the route alternates between elevated sections, ground-level roads and narrow lanes.

Cancelling the project will require the authorities to demolish the stations. The Roads and Highways Department (RHD) plans to relocate the lifts and other equipment for use elsewhere.

People travelling from greater Mymensingh, northern Bangladesh and Tangail use this road regularly. During construction, accidents involving cranes and other incidents also claimed seven lives.

Flawed planning from the outset

Relevant sources said the authorities launched the project before completing a comprehensive feasibility study and design. After construction began, they discovered that the project area lacked an adequate drainage system, causing water to accumulate.

The authorities had also failed to plan in advance for relocating utility lines belonging to various service providers. Nor had they arranged alternative traffic management measures to keep vehicles moving while construction continued on the busy road.

Three government agencies were responsible for implementing the project: the Roads and Highways Department (RHD), the Bridges Division and the Local Government Engineering Department (LGED). In 2013, the authorities established the Dhaka Bus Rapid Transit Company to operate the BRT service.

The company currently has 18 employees, including its managing director. However, its activities remain limited because the authorities never purchased the dedicated buses. The government has now decided to dissolve the company and bring its functions under the RHD.

The BUET report recommended holding the consultants who prepared the feasibility study and designed the project, as well as the government officials involved in its planning and implementation, accountable.

It also recommended reviewing the roles of the funding agencies, the project steering committee, the Implementation Monitoring and Evaluation Division (IMED) and the Planning Commission.

However, the Bangladesh Institute of Planners (BIP) has also raised concerns about the financial implications of cancelling the project.

At a seminar last year, the organisation argued that cancelling the project would be inappropriate when only 3 per cent of the infrastructure work remained unfinished.

According to its estimates, removing the stations, ramps and escalators and compensating contractors could cost more than Tk 10 billion (1,000 crore) if the government cancels the project.

Ishraque’s resignation accepted, gazette issued
item.description:
Ishraque Hossain’s resignation as state minister for liberation war affairs has been accepted. A gazette issued by the Cabinet Division on Tuesday said the President has accepted Ishraque’s resignation.

On Monday around 2:30 pm, Ishraque announced his resignation as state minister at a press conference at the National Press Club in the capital. According to rules, the President accepts a resignation after it is submitted. The Cabinet Division then issues a gazette to this effect.

Ishraque loses ministerial position due to showy display of power

Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) leader Ishraque is the member of parliament for Dhaka-6. On Saturday afternoon, he took part in an anti-drug drive in Gendaria, within his constituency, while carrying a firearm. After a video of the operation spread on social media, it sparked widespread discussion and criticism.

This action of his while serving as the state minister for liberation war affairs caused discontent within the BNP and the government. Multiple government sources confirmed to Prothom Alo that Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Sunday instructed him to resign.

I apologise if I made a mistake, but I did nothing wrong: Ishraque

After news of the resignation order emerged, Ishraque denied it. His side issued a protest and threatened legal action also. He eventually announced his resignation as state minister at a press conference at the National Press Club on Monday afternoon. Later in the evening, a high level source in the Cabinet Division told Prothom Alo that it has received Ishraque’s resignation letter.

Ahmed Azam Khan currently serves as the minister for liberation war affairs, with Ishraque having served as his state minister. Excluding the prime minister, the Cabinet had 26 full ministers and 24 state ministers. Following Ishraque’s resignation, the number of state ministers has fallen to 23.
